threads.question:
Thank you for your response. I understand what information needs to be included and my question is in regards to entering the information within the e-APR. Can work history (for the past ten years) that is not awarded points be inputted within the Personal History section (instead of under the Work History section) so that a document upload is not generated in the checklist? Wed Jan 06 2016 15:15:51 GMT-0500 (Eastern Standard Time)
Dear
In response to your question, when candidates are invited to apply, at the eAPR stage they are required to provide a complete history with respect to their work experience, education and other activities as part of their application for permanent residence (APR). Applicants should include their work experience for the last 10 years. Please note that when completing the application for permanent residence all activities that have taken place since the age of 18 have to be reported under the Personal History section as this is also a requirement for the application for permanent residence. Please also take into consideration that there is a system limit of 30 entries. Should the Personal History contains more entries we require that the additional information be added to a separate document and uploaded in the field "Letter of explanation".

Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox
threads.answer:
Dear
Thank you for your query.
In response to your question, you are correct in your assumption that work history (for the past ten years) that is not awarded points can be inputted within the Personal History section (instead of under the Work History section). As prior indicated, please note that at the eAPR stage an applicant is required to provide a complete history with respect to their work experience, education and other activities as part of their application for permanent residence (APR) for the last 10 years. Per section 11.2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, applicants must support with evidence all information claimed in their Express Entry profile which was the basis for the awarding of Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points and an invitation to apply under a given program. For example, as no CRS points are awarded for work experience in NOC C or D occupations, proof of such work experience would not be required as part of the work history section of the application for permanent residence. However, an applicant is required to include their lower-skilled work experience when completing the personal history section of their application to account for their overall work experience, education and other activities for purposes of admissibility screening.
We hope this information will assist you. Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

et Ciloyenneé Canada
threads.answer:
As part of (IRCC)'s Modernization Agenda, IRCC has changed the way it operates by moving away from paper files, by centralizing application intake, and by optimizing global workload distribution in-Canada and abroad. More and more applicants are able to apply online and pay electronically. Applications are now processed where capacity exists, resulting in improved efficiencies. Because of these changes, IRCC is centralizing more of its work from abroad to Canada.
As a result, it is no longer relevant for clients to have the processing times by mission, as this is not the best indicator of how long it may take for a file to be processed. The processing times posted on the IRCC website are based on 8oth percentile, meaning that the processing times posted show that 80% of applications finalized are processed within X months or less. Applicants or their representatives may also use the on-line Client Application Status (CAS) tool to obtain further information on the status of an application.

threads.subject: Approved Response-RE: Interpretation of Regulation 87(1)(3)(a) and (c) - work experience towards CEC-REP- 2016-0001
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
Could you please clarify the interpretation of regulation 87(1)(3)(a) and (c)
Question
Does the work experience gained after an international student has finished his study program but before he has obtained the Post Graduated Work Permit count towards work experience to qualify under the Canadian Experience Program?
I believe it does. Below is my interpretation of the related regulations:
- (a)any period of employment during which the foreign national was engaged in full-time study shall not be included in calculating a period of work experience;
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
Information dscloseddr e es InfomationAct My interpretation: The international student is not engaged in full time study anymore once he has finished the study program. The regulation states the action of studying, and not the legal instrument that allows him to study.
- (c)the foreign national must have had temporary resident status during their period of work experience and any period of full-time study or training
My interpretation: The international student must have a temporary resident status, which could be work permit or study permit which allow him to work full time after he has finished the study program. It does not limit to a work permit status during their period of work experience.
Thanks in advance for your assistance and Happy New Year!
Regards,
threads.answer:
Thank you for your inquiry.
For a student who has graduated from a Canadian post-secondary institution, only work experience gained after graduation will count towards meeting the work experience requirement under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC).
As per the Program Delivery Instructions published on our website as a courtesy to stakeholders, any period of employment during which the applicant was engaged in full-time study will not be included in calculating the period of qualifying work experience under the CEC (e.g., work experience gained through co-op work permits, off-campus work permits while a full-time student and on-campus work permits). The wording of the instructions recognizes the possibility for a CEC applicant to gain qualifying work experience in Canada through authorized off-campus work, particularly for short periods of time during scheduled academic breaks or during transition to a post-graduate work permit.
However, in all cases, the onus is on the applicant to satisfy an officer that they were not engaged in full-time studies during the period of work experience claimed in their application.
Sincerely, Immigration Representatives Inbox

threads.answer:
Question: I wanted to write to ask whether a study permit would be required in the following circumstance. I have a few clients (graphic artists) who have valid work permits (usually 2 year LMIA based work permits) working full time in Vancouver in skilled positions. These foreign workers would like to take one course a semester or each year at a local film / visual effects schools. They are not •genrolled• h in a diploma or certification program per se, but the credits received from taking these courses could technically lead to a diploma at some point (would take several years).
I have reviewed the policy guidelines and the only reference I can find states as follows:
If you wish to study in a short-term course or program
You do not need a study permit if you plan to take a course or program in Canada that lasts six months or less. You must complete the course or program within the period authorized for your stay in Canada.
[http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/study/study-who.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/study/study-who.asp)
The issue is that these foreign workers are not eligible for a •gstudy permit-h as they are not accepted into a program of study as they will be taking only 1 or 2 courses per year.
If you could provide guidance in this circumstance, it would be greatly appreciated.
Answer:
In general foreign nationals are required to obtain a study permit to engage in any academic, professional, vocational training at a designated learning institution in Canada. Subsection 188(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) outline the circumstances under which a foreign national may study in Canada without a study permit.
For example, foreign nationals, including work permit holders, may study without a study permit if the duration of their course or program of studies will be completed within 6 months or less, as stipulated under paragraph 188(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.
Foreign nationals who hold a valid work permit and intend to study in a program that is longer than 6 months, may apply for a study permit from within Canada under paragraph 215(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.

threads.subject: Approved Response-RE: Express Entry Work Experience-REP-2016-0050
threads.question:
Hello,
If a student works full-time during the summer terms, is this experience included in the one year of work experience required for consideration under the Canadian Experience Class? The student did not engage in work to obtain any school credit, and the position was a skilled position, i.e. a research assistant. I understand that FSW requires continuous employment, but this is not the case for CEC. CEC also does not include work done for school credit, for example a co-op position, but is a paid summer position also disqualified?
Kindly,
Page 355
is withheld pursuant to section est retenue en vertu de l'article
of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
threads.answer:
Thank you for your inquiry.
For a student who has graduated from a Canadian post-secondary institution, only work experience gained after graduation will count towards meeting the work experience requirement under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC).
As per the Program Delivery Instructions published on our website as a courtesy to stakeholders, any period of employment during which the applicant was engaged in full-time study will not be included in calculating the period of qualifying work experience under the CEC (e.g., work experience gained through co-op work permits, off-campus work permits while a full-time student and on-campus work permits). The wording of the instructions recognizes the possibility for a CEC applicant to gain qualifying work experience in Canada through authorized off-campus work, particularly for short periods of time during scheduled academic breaks or during transition to a post-graduate work permit.
However, in all cases, the onus is on the applicant to satisfy an officer that they were not engaged in full-time studies during the period of work experience claimed in their application.

threads.subject: Approved Response-RE: ITA and points for LMIA-REP-2016-0078
threads.question:
Yang, Katherine (CA-Toronto)
Dear Sir/Madam:
We have a client who was issued an ITA in December. He has an LMIA-based work permit and received 600 points, however, his work permit expires after the ITA is due.
Please advise if the LMiA-based work permit is required to be valid during the processing of the application to substantiate the 600 points, or if as long as the application is submitted before the LMiA-based work permit expires, they can still substantiate the 600 points.
Thank you.
Page 359
is withheld pursuant to section est retenue en vertu de l'article
of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
threads.answer:
Thank you for your inquiry.
Candidates who declare in their Express Entry profile that they have a valid job offer, supported by an LMlA in a skilled occupation, will automatically receive an additional 600 points towards their Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score. A candidate who declares that they have a valid job offer because they are authorized to work in Canada on an LMlA-backed work permit in a skilled occupation with an offer of arranged employment from their current employer must do so because their work permit is valid at the time they submit their profile.
If invited to apply, to remain eligible for the 600 points for such a declared job offer, the candidate's work permit must continue to be valid or they must have applied for an LMlA-backed work permit before the expiry date of their previous one (and therefore have implied status) at the time their application for permanent residence is received.
Taking your example, provided the applicant had supported their claim of having a valid job offer and met the minimum entry criteria for Express Entry at the time of application, they would have demonstrated with evidence that they had maintained the qualifications which led to them being invited to apply and were entitled to the 600 additional points received towards their CRS score for an offer of arranged employment. The applicant would therefore meet the requirements of section 11.2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. Their entitlement to the 600 additional points is fixed at that point in time.
The applicant must ensure that they remain in status and only work with proper authorization at all times, and must hold a valid work permit or be otherwise authorized to work in Canada at the time the permanent resident visa, if any, is issued.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Inbox

threads.answer:

As you've noted, the onus is on the candidate to assess their work experience against the National Occupational Classification (NOC) and identify the NOC codes for the occupations in which they claim qualifying experience, including for the primary occupation they chose to specify in their Express Entry profile.
If invited to apply, the individual must be prepared to substantiate all work experience claimed in their profile and provide evidence that their claimed experience corresponds to the occupational description(s) as set out in the NOC codes they have specified.

In a case where the only change has been the duration requested (e.g. the compliance filing says six months but the employer now needs the employee for nine months), does the employer need to complete a new compliance filing and request a refund for the previous one, or can the applicant still rely on the compliance filing as there has been no change in the conditions of employment (occupation, salary, location) and the only change is the duration?

If you want to modify information in a submitted offer, you must:

threads.subject: Prevailing wage-REP-2015-3282
threads.question:
Thanks, but the question is related to inter company transfers, specialized knowledge. If the prevailing wage increases does the employer have an obligation to increase the foreign workers wage immediately to match the prevailing wage?
Regards, Peter
threads.answer:
The temporary foreign worker program (TFWP) is unique in that its delivery relies on the close cooperation of three different departments (Employment and Social Development Canada [ESDC], Citizenship and Immigration Canada [CIC] and Canada
Border Services Agency [CBSA]).
Under the TFWP, ESDC is responsible for issuing Labour Market Impact Assessments (LMIA) when requested by employers and conducting compliance activities to ensure employers follow rules once they are granted access to the Program. Under both the TFWP and International Mobility Program (IMP), CIC is responsible for the administration of selection and processing in the issuance of temporary resident visas and work permits to qualified applicants, as well as the refusal of unqualified applicants. The CBSA is responsible for assessing whether applicants are admissible to Canada before issuing work permits to foreign nationals at Canada's ports of entry.
IRCC does not have a policy or requirement for employers to meet the prevailing wage. This is a requirement of obtaining an LMIA and ESDC applies it.
IRCC does not require proactive notification of changes to the employer conditions (e.g. wages, working conditions, etc). The IRPR require that an employer provide documentation at the time of inspection to show that they met the conditions or proof of their justification (as per R203(1.1) ) if they believe they did not meet the conditions.
Since the prevailing wage program is led by ESDC, we suggest that you refer to the ESDC website where more details regarding the changes to prevailing wages are available: [http://www.esdc.gc.ca/eng/jobs/foreign_workers/high_low](http://www.esdc.gc.ca/eng/jobs/foreign_workers/high_low) wage/low_wage/index.shtml
If the information you are requesting is not available, please contact ESDC for further assistance.

[mailto: ]
Thank you for your question on the matter of prevailing wage for a temporary foreign worker.
The prevailing wage is an issue regulated by applicable federal or territorial regulations.
You will find the following information on the Employment and Social Development Canada website:
Employers must ensure the wage offered to the foreign worker is not below any:
- Applicable federal or provincial/territorial minimum wage rates; or Wage schedules set by provincial/territorial legislation (e.g. Manitoba Construction Industry Wages Act).
Employers offering a wage that is below the prevailing wage rate will be considered as not meeting the labour market factor for the assessment of wages and therefore, will be issued a negative Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA).
Further information can be found on the ESDC website: [http://www.esdc.gc.ca/eng/jobs/foreign_workers/higher_skilled/permanent/index.shtml](http://www.esdc.gc.ca/eng/jobs/foreign_workers/higher_skilled/permanent/index.shtml)
The employer is not required to wait until the extension of the work permit in order to modify the wage.
I trust this information will be of assistance.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Inbox

threads.subject: Question about Place ofLanding-REP-2016-0084
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam:
If an applicant applies for permanent residence through the FS WP or CEC, and indicates a province of destination other than Quebec (say BC), but at the time of landing indicates that they intend on residing in a different province (again, other than Quebec, say Ontario), is this a ground for denying the applicant landing?
Respectfully yours,
串 Lnomdn
threads.answer:
Thank you for your inquiry.
Membership in the Federal Skilled Worker Class and Canadian Experience Class is restricted to persons who intend to reside anywhere in Canada other than the province of Quebec.
An officer must be satisfied that an applicant under either of these federal immigration classes intends to reside outside of Quebec. Provided this is the case, an applicant is free to indicate any province other than Quebec as their intended province of destination, both at the time of application and landing.

threads.subject: Question-CEC PR applicant, loss of valid LMIA Offer-REP-2016-0089 - Due by 15-Feb-16
threads.question:
Dear CIC
I would like clarification on Canadian Experience Class applicants with a valid LMIA permanent job offer. This refers to CEC applicants with a PR application in process, who loses their valid job offer.
Under CEC, there is no requirement to have a valid job offer. Under Express Entry, an applicant with a qualifying job offer tied to an LMIA can receive 600 points.
My question is: If a CEC applicant loses his job while his PR application is in process, does he no longer qualify as a permanent resident because he does not have a valid job offer? Or, since his points were locked in at the time of submission, he can still qualify and be approved as a CEC applicant.
Linformation divulguée en vertu de la loi sur l’accés à Finformation The confusion lies in the fact the points are locked in at the time of submitting the PR, and CEC applicants do not require a valid job offer to be approved under the CEC requirements.
Please advise
中 and Cizenship Canada
threads.answer:
Thank you for your enquiry.
In Express Entry, an applicant's information and Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score are locked-in when an invitation to apply (ITA) is issued and when an applicant submits their electronic application for permanent residence (e-APR). An officer will conduct an assessment under A11.2 to ensure that the applicant meets the minimum entry criteria and possesses the qualifications for which they received their CRS score at the time of ITA and e-APR. As long as the applicant continues to meet all of the requirements when their e-APR is submitted, they will pass the A11.2 assessment and their CRS score will not be recalculated in the future.
However, any change in circumstance could potentially impact program eligibility. All applicants have an obligation to notify CiC whenever a change occurs that could affect their application. If the applicant loses their job or their job offer becomes invalid while their e-APR is in process, they must notify CiC of such, so that an officer can determine if they continue to meet the requirements of the program under which they were invited to apply. With regards to your specific question, while the loss of a job offer after application submission would not usually impact an applicant's ability to meet Canadian Experience Class requirements, IRCC will consider each application on its own merits with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision.
For more information, please see the CiC website: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/perm/express/refuse.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/perm/express/refuse.asp)

threads.question:

1. available,
2. transferable and
3. not committed to debts or other obligations.
Further, what is an applicant to do if they have only had the account open for 4-5 months (and have saved the $12,164 in that time), since they won't be able to show the ‘average balance for the past 6 months'?

Page 2

of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
threads.answer:
Ms There is nothing to preclude funds held in an offshore account from counting towards meeting the settlement fund
requirement. As you've noted, an applicant must satisfy the officer that they have sufficient available and transferable funds, unencumbered by debts or other obligations. These funds must be available to the applicant both at the time of application and at the time a permanent resident visa (if any) is issued. Officers must be satisfied that funds are legally accessible to the foreign national for their free and exclusive use to support settlement upon arrival.
As for your second question, applicants are asked to submit proof of funds consisting of official letter(s) from financial institution(s) which include the current balance of each account as well as the average balance in the past six months, as both current and historical balances are indicators of their access to sufficient available funds. If an applicant submits evidence of funds held in an account that has been active for less than 6 months, their application will not generally be rejected as incomplete on that basis alone. Should their application be placed into processing, they should be prepared to provide evidence of average balances over a longer period to demonstrate stable access to sufficient funds.
Sincerely, Immigration Representatives Mailbox

On a permanent residence application to be submitted by a provincial nominee, is there a requirement to include a processing fee payment, or Right of Permanent Residence fee payment, for a non-accompanying spouse from whom the principal applicant is
separated but not yet divorced?

threads.answer:
Dear Robbie Sheffman,
As indicated in IRPR 295 (1): The following fees are payable for processing an application for a permanent resident visa: (c) if the application is made by a person as a member of any other class or by a person referred to in section 71 (ii) in respect of a family member of the principal applicant who is a spouse or common-law partner, $550. As well, IRPR 5 indicates: Excluded relationships: For the purposes of these Regulations, a foreign national shall not be considered (b) the spouse of a person if (ii) the person has lived separate and apart from the foreign national for at least one year and is the common-law partner of another person.
The manual OP 2 Processing Members of the Family Class, section "5.38. What happens if the common-law partner (principal
applicant) is married to another person?" provides additional information:
"Officers must be satisfied that a principal applicant is separated from and no longer cohabits with a legal spouse. This evidence may be in the form of a signed formal declaration that the marriage has ended and that the person has entered into a common-law relationship. An officer may require that the person produce other written evidence of a formal separation or of a breakdown of the marriage. Acceptable documents include a separation agreement, a court order in respect of custody of children identifying the fact of the marriage breakdown, documents removing the legally married spouse(s) from insurance policies or will as beneficiaries (a "change of beneficiary" form). In the above circumstances, the legal spouse of the principal applicant need not be examined and will not be considered a member of the family class if the applicant later attempts to sponsor this spouse. [See R117(9)(d)]. Notes in CAIPS
should indicate that the applicant was aware of the consequences of non-examination."

threads.subject: Minimum Necessary Income-REP-2016-0169
threads.question:
Can the income earned in Canada by a permanent resident prior to becoming a permanent resident be used to meet the Minimum Necessary Income requirement?
Specifically, if my client became a permanent resident in 2015 and applies to sponsor her parents in 2016, can she use income earned in 2014 while employed on a work permit to meet the MNI requirement for that year? Or, does she need to have been a permanent resident to include that income?

threads.answer:
Good day,
The sponsor's total income would be assessed on the basis of a Notice of Assessment (NOA) or equivalent document issued by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) for each of the three consecutive taxation years preceding the date the application was submitted.

threads.subject: Question regarding PR Card renewal and travel to Canada / ETA system / citizen of visa exempt country-REP- 2015-3234
threads.question:
Hi. Question related to PRs who are from visa exempt countries other than the United States -so assume for this question the PR is a citizen of Sweden.
PR Card renewals are presently taking 6 months or more according to CIC posted timelines.
As I understand it (but please confirm) Canadian PRs cannot obtain an ETA because by definition ETAs are for temporary residents/visitors.
The ETA regime is mandatory as of March 15 (just in time for March Break which will cause added travel chaos at that busy time, but that is merely a rhetorical comment ©).
In the past, a PR from a visa exempt country would usually be able to board a commercial flight to Canada EVEN WHERE THE PR CARD HAD LAPSED based on their passport. threads.answer:

As of March 15, 2016, although visa exempt foreign nationals will require an eTA, if they are a permanent resident of Canada they will not eligible for an eTA. For permanent residents outside Canada who is not in possession of a PR card, they can apply for a Permanent Resident Travel Document. Permanent Residents must submit their application at a visa application centre and may submit their application to their country of nationality or the country where they have been legally admitted. threads.subject: Study permits and studies-REP-2016-0106
threads.question:
1. If an FN defers the first period of study, are they determined to be non-compliant? Obviously, if the FN had no intention to study at all, then they are not compliant with the conditions of the permit. However, 220.1 makes no reference as to when an FN must begin their studies. One would assume that the individual should begin studies as outlined in the acceptance letter, but R220.1 makes no definite statement to this effect. It would appear that R222 applies after a permit holder completes their studies but it makes no reference to someone who has not started their studies.
2. If the FN defers the first period of study, it is our understanding that they would not be eligible for off campus employment on the basis the conditions for off campus work include being ‘a full-time student,' 'be enrolled...,' and 'be studying..' Is this correct?
Infomat dioss omonAct
3. If the FN defers the first period of study, and this is, in fact, non-compliance, does this have any repercussions on the spouse / common-law partner who possesses an open work permit?
Thanks!
Citoenneté Canada
threads.answer:
As per A29(2), a temporary resident must comply with any conditions imposed under the regulations and with any requirements under this Act, must leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay and may re-enter Canada only if their authorization provides for re-entry. One of these conditions, as per R220.1, is that once in Canada, holders of a Study Permit must actively pursue their course or program of study. Therefore, the student in this scenario may be determined to be non-compliant.
2.If the FN defers the first period of study, it is our understanding that they would not be eligible for off campus employment on the basis the conditions for off campus work include being 'a full-time student,' 'be enrolled..,' and 'be studying...' Is this correct?

As per R186v, A foreign national may work in Canada without a work permit if they are the holder of a study permit and
(i) they are a full-time student enrolled at a designated learning institution as defined in section 211.1, (ii) the program in which they are enrolled is a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program, or a vocational training program at the secondary level offered in Quebec, in each case, of a duration of six months or more that leads to a degree, diploma or certificate, and (iii) although they are permitted to engage in full-time work during a regularly scheduled break between academic sessions, they work no more than 20 hours per week during a regular academic session;
3. If the FN defers the first period of study, and this is, in fact, non-compliance, does this have any repercussions on the spouse / common-law partner who possesses an open work permit?

No repercussion on the spouse/CLP's document.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Inbox

Only under exceptional circumstances have salaries for Post-doctoral Fellows surpassed $60,000 but never through an unscheduled salary increase. threads.answer:
This is in response to your question sent to the Immigration Representatives mailbox on January 12, 2016.
Hello
Question:
Please advise if this is allowable under the IMP program or if a LMIA is required due to such a large salary increase.
Response:
Typically, any substantial change from the Offer of Employment must be justified as per subsection 203(1.1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). An officer may find that a change in an employee contract that increases the salary is justified under R203(1.1) in that it is similar to a change in the provisions of a collective agreement. In addition, an increase in wages may result in a finding that the employer did not provide “substantially the same” wages if the increase would have affected the ability of the foreign national to qualify for the LMIA-exemption. Wages under the International Mobility Program must meet the minimum wage requirement in the province of employment as per the condition to meet federal or provincial laws. Wages paid that are higher than those in the offer of employment, it may indicate a change in duties that would mean a different occupation than offered. In cases where the employer has promoted or otherwise changed the foreign worker's duties, the foreign worker must receive a new Offer of Employment and work permit prior to implementing the change. If a new work permit for the promotion or change in occupation has not been previously approved and the temporary foreign worker is found to be working in an occupation other than what was stated on the Offer of Employment, this may constitute non-compliance by the employer. Please note that proactive notification of salary changes are not required under the International Mobility Program (Led by ). However, this information may be requested along with justification for the salary change when the foreign worker applies for an extension of their work permit or a new foreign worker applies for a work permit for the same employer.
Foreign workers are also subject to other federal (such as ESDC who leads the Temporary Foreign Workers Program) and provincial or territorial legislative and regulatory requirements. Employers should also meet those requirements for compliance purposes.
I hope this answers your question.

It is important to note that the requirements for a qualifying offer of arranged employment differ between the Ministerial Instructions Respecting the Express Entry System (Mis) and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.

threads.subject: Approved Response-RE: Does a soldier under VFA acquire Canadian experience while working in Canada? - REP-2016-0248
threads.question:
We represent a soldier in Canada under R186(d) (foreign military personnel) who is interested in applying for permanent residency through Express Entry.
Does work experience gained in Canada while working for the forces of a foreign government as a soldier make an applicant eligible for the Canadian Experience Class and eligible for additional ‘points' under Express Entry?
I’ve reviewed the Ministerial Instructions for EE, the Regulations, and the policy references for FSW and CEC. I can't
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
L'nmon find anything that says that working for the armed forces of a foreign government would exclude him from CEC or from claiming points for Canadian work experience.
I would appreciate if you could clarify this matter for me. If, in fact, work done as a soldier for a foreign government under R186(d) is not considered ‘Canadian work', I would appreciate the legislative/policy reference for this.
Best,
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your inquiry.
An individual does not need to hold a work permit to qualify under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC). Individuals who are authorized to work in Canada under section 186 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations are eligible if invited to apply under the CEC through Express Entry, but must provide documentation with their application establishing that they had legal temporary status in Canada.
Foreign nationals who are members of the armed forces of a country that is a designated state for the purposes of the Visiting Forces Act (VFA), including a person who has been designated as a civilian component of those armed forces, may be admitted to Canada as workers exempt from the work permit requirements pursuant to paragraph 186(d) of the Regulations. These workers are documented on visitor records when seeking entry to Canada to perform official duties under the VFA for a duration of six months or more. The visitor record would serve to demonstrate that they had temporary resident status and were authorized to work in Canada.
Notwithstanding the references to 'Canadian Forces'in the National Occupational Classification (NOC), foreign military members do not need to have served as members of the Canadian forces in order for qualifying experience per NOC 0433 or NOC 4313 job descriptions to count towards the work experience requirement under the CEC, or for purposes of claiming Comprehensive Ranking System points for 'Canadian work experience' under Express Entry.
Assuming that such an individual invited to apply under the CEC meets all program requirements and passes the A11.2 assessment, their electronic application for permanent residence would be processed without regard to their “status” with the foreign military service (i.e. they would not be required to furnish discharge papers in order for their application to be finalized).
Sincerely, Immigration Representatives Inbox

threads.subject: Visiteur en sabbatique-REP-2016-0073 - Due by 11-Feb-16
threads.question:
Bonjour, Je vous seriez reconnaissante si vous pouviez clarifier le statut que les visiteurs en sabbatique au Canada doivent avoir. J’étais surprise de trouver dans les directives d’Immigration Canada, dans la description des « Professeurs invités » la remarque suivante; « Les professeurs invités comprennent également les personnes qui, au cours d’une année sabbatique, font de la recherche en collaboration avec un établissement d’enseignement postsecondaire du Canada ». Ceci laisse croire que ceux en congé sabbatique peuvent être délivrés un permis de travail (sans ElMT) en application de la dispense C-22. Ma
compréhension était que ceux qui sont autofinancés (donc que ne reçoivent aucune rémunération de l’institution
canadienne) et qui simplement visitent pour travailler dans leurs propres projets de recherche (que, évidement, ont un intérêt pour l'institution qui l’accueille) ne sont pas en train d'entrer dans le marché du travail et peuvent être admis comme visiteurs. Il me semble que la phrase que j'ai cité se prête à confusion et devrait être clarifiée. Ce qu’elle devrait vouloir dire est que les professeurs étrangers qui viennent au Canada durant leur sabbatique et qui vont contribuer aux projets de recherche d’une organisation canadienne qui fait la recherche (et qui, normalement, recevront une type de compensation de l’organisation canadienne et qui vont enseigner au Canada pendant la sabbatique, par exemple) peuvent être admis comme « professeurs invités » sous la dispense C-22. Par contre ceux qui ne prennent rien de l’institution canadienne (pas un sou sur aucun concept) sauf une place pour s’assoir pendant un an et la possibilité d’échanger avec les chercheurs de l'organisation canadienne, qui viennent avecleur propre projet de recherche et financés totalement pour leur université
étrangère clairement ne rentrent pas dans le marché du travail. Ils sont visiteurs. 100%. De la même manière qui sont visiteurs les étudiants/chercheurs financés intégralement de l’étranger. Pourriez-vous clarifier svp?
Merci beaucoup!
Salutations,
and Citizenship Caneda
threads.answer:
Nous sommes désolés de ne pas vous avoir répondu plus tôt.
Les instructions en ce qui concerne le code de dispense C22 - Professeurs invités ne parlent pas de rémunération parce que le salaire des professeurs en sabbatique continue généralement d’être payé par leur université d’origine. C’est la convention qui est simplement implicite dans les instructions
Même si les instructions ne parlent pas de salaire, elles parlent de sabbatique. Le professeur étranger doit démontrer à l’agent de visa que le poste qu’il va occuper ou la recherche qu’il va faire dans l’université canadienne se fait dans le cadre de sa sabbatique (avec une lettre de l’université du pays d’origine et de l’université hôte au Canada).
En principe, on peut émettre un permis de travail à un professeur en sabbatique qui vient faire de la recherche au Canada sans être payé. En autant qu’il prouve que c’est lié à sa sabbatique (les universités octroient des sabbatiques seulement pour faire de la recherche ou prendre un poste qui contribuent à leur développement dans leur domaine d’expertise).
Par contre, on peut émettre un visa de visiteur commercial à un chercheur étranger autofinancé. Mais pour ça, il ne suffit pas d’être autofinancé; il faut convaincre l’agent que le type de travail effectué ne constitue pas du travail' selon la définition du Règlement sur l’immigration et la protection des réfugiés. Si l’activité proposée n’est pas considérée comme un « travail » au sens de la définition, l’agent peut demander un permis de travail. Un visa de visiteur commercial est généralement octroyé pour telles activités : assister à une réunion, une conférence, une convention ou une foire commerciale; bref, des activités qui n’impliquent pas du travail trop concret.
J’espère que cela répond à votre question.

threads.subject: Approved Response-RE: Question regarding work history in EE-REP-2016-0176
threads.question:
Dear Officer,
In the following, we are only referring to qualifying as a member of the FSW, FST, and CEC classes in the context of employment. We understand that there are other factors involved, such as English / French testing, ECAs, admissibility, etc.
In summary, IRPR 75(2)(a) states that an FN is a skilled worker if within the 10 years preceding the application the FN has at least one year of qualifying full-time work experience.
In summary, IRPR 87.1(2)(a) states that an FN is a member of the CEC class if within the three years preceding the application the FN has at least one year of qualifying full-time work experience.
In summary, IRPR 87.2(3)(b) states that an FN is a member of the FST class if within the five years preceding the application the FN has at least two years of qualifying full-time work experience
In an application for PR under EE, specifically during the preparation of the eAPR, we are asked to disclose work history and personal history. However, the online prompts do not tell us how much work history is required in this section. Personal history clearly states 10 years or since you were 18. As some individuals may have employment history that goes back 30 years, this can be extremely cumbersome, particularly since we are required to obtain reference letters for each period of employment if the employment is entered under the employment history. In many cases, this becomes virtually impossible
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
the further removed we get from the current date.
As such, our question is as follows:
1. Following the issuance of an ITA, are we required to enter ALL work history in the work history section of the eAPR or just the work history that meets the minimum criteria for the category under which the ITA was issued?
The online description of employment history seems to imply that the only work history that must be listed in this section is history that would be used for the points calculation / confirmation. In the case of a FSW then, it seems that while it would be wise to list at least 10 years of history, to make sure that if a period of time is found to be ineligible you still have qualifying time from with to draw from and remain eligible, that it is not necessary to do so. It seems that a client could only list 5 years for their past 10 year history and would still satisfy the purpose of the employment section.
We're more concerned with the possibility of making a misrepresentation by omission if we don't disclose the entire work
history of an individual.
Regards,
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your inquiry.
No set period is specified in the work history section of the Express Entry profile, as the skilled work experience element of the minimum entry criteria differs between each of the federal immigration programs subject to Express Entry.
It is in each candidate's best interest to provide as much information as possible in the work history section of their profile to ensure they maximize their Comprehensive Ranking System points, and that all of their work experience is assessed against the minimum entry criteria of all eligible programs. However, a candidate who wishes to declare only that work experience which meets the minimum entry criteria for a specific program in the work history section of their profile may do so. If invited to apply, the information declared in the work history section of their profile would be carried forward to their application, and any other work experience which is not relevant to program eligibility or the awarding of CRS points would then have to be included in the personal history section of their application for purposes of admissibility screening.
Daníara Pelchat Permanent Resident Program Delivery Division de la prestation du programme des résidents permanents NHQ-Operational Management and Coordination AC-Gestion opérationnelle et coordination |

I have a case where an individual has been nominated by the province of Alberta and has submitted an application for permanent residence under the PNP program to IRCC. As well the individual has applied for permanent residence to IRCC under the PNP program and has since obtained an open work permit by applying under the BOWP program.
The employee is now considering changing employers and occupation. He is currently on an open work permit with no employer or occupation restrictions. The open work permit was obtained with the support of the acknowledgment of receipt received in support of the PNP permanent resident application. The new position and employer would still be in Alberta. The nomination certificate that was received from the AlNP even though it was submitted through the employer as the worker had a job offer indicates that there are no restrictions to employment.
At this time we are concerned about what the consequences may be, if any, if he changes employers when the employer they want to leave nominated them through the AINP program. Would changing occupations and employers affect the outcome of the permanent resident application?

threads.answer:
Dear
This is in reply to your enquiry on whether a change of circumstances in a provincial nominee occupation related to the issuance of an open work permit would negatively affect a permanent residence application under the provincial nominee program (PNP).
If there is no indication on a nomination letter that employment restrictions exist as conditions of the nomination, a provincial nominee is eligible for a bridging open work permit (BOwP). When such an open work permit is issued, the individual is then authorized by (IRCC) to work for a different employer in the province or territory of nomination. More details on BOwPs can be found under International Mobility Program: Provincial nominees and permanent residence applications -Bridging open work permits for certain federal economic class applicants. You may also consult the Help Centre question Does my work permit allow me to work for any employer in Canada? as well as the program delivery instructions International Mobility Program: Open work permit which contains sections on types of open work permits and the conditions imposed.
That being said, it is the responsibility of the nominee to ensure that they abide by the terms and conditions that may have been imposed by the province or territory issuing the nomination, which may not necessarily appear on a nomination letter. We would advise that you contact the nominating provincial or territorial government regarding whether the change in employer and/or occupation could result in the withdrawal of the nomination certificate. It is possible that the province or territory may re-evaluate the nomination in light of the new information received to determine if the individual still meets their criteria. If the nomination certificate were to be withdrawn in that case, IRCC would refuse the permanent residence application due to the foreign national not being a member of the provincial nominee class as per R87(2)(a).

threads.subject: Temporary Resident Permit-REP-2016-0115
threads.question:
Anastasia Koutouzov, Ms.
Dear Madam/Sir,
I have a student who was issued a Temporary Resident Permit (TRP) at a port of entry because he had a valid study permit but did not have a valid Temporary Resident Visa (TRV) when entering Canada. His TRP will expire in March 2016.
In December, he left Canada and applied for a new study permit and TRV at the visa office that serves his nationality. His study permit application was approved and he entered Canada with a valid TRV and was issued a new study permit. Both documents are valid until August 2017. The border officer told him that his TRP remained valid until March 2016 and that when he would be renewing his documents (study permit and TRV), he would not need to renew his TRP since he now had a valid TRV.
My concern is that in the past I have seen Immigration Canada refuse to issue the extension of a study permit or work permit on the basis that the foreign national has not applied to extend their temporary resident permit even though the person has rectify their immigration situation and no longer fails to meet the requirements of IRPR.
Furthermore, on your website you state:
TRP holders must:
- leave Canada before the TRP's expiry date or upon cancellation of their TRP by an officer
- apply for a subsequent TRP before the expiry of their TRP if they want to maintain their temporary resident status in Canada
- apply for and obtain a counterfoil to allow them to return to Canada if all of the following applies: o they are from a country whose citizens require a temporary resident visa o they have authorization to re-enter Canada.
TRP holders who do not comply with the provisions of IRPA or its Regulations, or whose circumstances change, may be subject to:
- cancellation of their TRP, an inadmissibility subsection A44 (1) report, and
- a removal order.
Therefore, if a foreign national has rectified their situation and is no longer in violation of IRPA, do they need to continue to renew their TRP or once they have rectified their situation they no longer need to renew their TRP?
If they do not renew their TRP will their application to extend their temporary resident documents (study or work permit) be refused?
More specifically, can the student in the situation mentioned above apply to renew their study permit or apply for a work permit without applying for an extension of their TRP since they now have a valid TRV issued by a visa office outside of Canada?
Thank you for taking the time to answer my questions.
With kind regards,
中 and Citizenship Caneda
threads.answer:
Good day,
Many thanks for your inquiry. To answer your questions, please see clarifications related to the type of TRP that was issued.
Situation 1: If a single-entry TRP was issued to the subject
As per R63.(b), a TRP is no longer valid if a TRP holder leaves Canada and does not have authorization to re-enter. Therefore, if, when examining an application, an officer discovers that a TRP holder has left Canada, the TRP is deemed cancelled. As such, if the subject was issued a single-entry TRP and left Canada without authorization to come back, his TRP is deemed cancelled and he does not need to renew his TRP and can apply for extension of his current document before its expiry.
Situation 2: If a multiple-entry TRP was issued to the subject
Before issuing the new TRV, the officer abroad should have had consulted the office where the TRP was issued explaining the change of circumstances and the intention to cancel the TRP. Now that the new TRV has been issued and that the student is not inadmissible anymore, IRCC will notify him that his TRP will be cancelled. After the TRP cancellation, the subject will be allowed to apply to extend his current valid TR documents without applying for a TRP extension.
With respect to your specific questions:
"If a foreign national has rectified their situation and is no longer in violation of IRPA, do they need to continue to renew their TRP or once they have rectified their situation they no longer need to renew their TRP?"
Answer: If the foreign national has rectified their situation and have been issued new temporary resident status documents, such as a TRV along with a study permit then the TRP does not have to be renewed.
"If they do not renew their TRP will their application to extend their temporary resident documents (study or work permit) be refused?"
Answer: Any request to extend temporary resident documents can be refused by the officer reviewing the application, as each application is considered on a case by case basis. However if the foreign national has rectified their situation through the issuance of a TRV and study permit, there is no requirement for them to renew their TRP, nor is a potential extension dependent on also renewing their TRP.
"Can the student in the situation mentioned above apply to renew their study permit or apply for a work permit without applying for an extension of their TRP since they now have a valid TRV issued by a visa office outside of Canada?“
Answer: Recognizing that it is difficult to comment on the specifics on any particular case, according to the regulations cited above, and the example you have shared the student can apply to extend or change their temporary status as long as they apply before the expiration of their current TRV and study permit.
Regards,
and Citizenship Caneda
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Inbox

The validity date is NOT the suggested duration of the visit. At the port of entry examination, CBSA officers determine the length of time temporary residents are authorized to stay in Canada.
Typically, when officers are satisfied that the foreign nationals are admissible, entry is granted for a six-month period
As per R190(3)(f), foreign nationals who are normally required to have TRVs to enter Canada are exempt from that requirement when they seek to re-enter, if, since leaving Canada after being authorized to enter as a temporary resident, they have only visited St. Pierre and Miquelon or the U.S. (including the Territories and Possessions of the U.S., but not including cruises that enter international waters) and:
- are returning within the initial period authorized by an officer; or
- are in possession of a valid VR, WP, SP or a TRP (authorizing re-entry) and are returning within the initial period authorized by an officer.
Following the information above, if a foreign national who has come to Canada as a visitor and was issued a 3 month Temporary Resident Visa, enters Canada before the expiration of their TRV and upon entry is not granted a Visitor Record nor is their passport stamped can we presume the following:
a) the duration of their authorized stay in Canada is 6 months, despite the expiration date of the their TRV, and
b) that the foreign national may travel to the United States and re-enter on their expired TRV without having to apply for a new TRV or Visitor Record as long as they re-enter Canada before the expiration of their 6 months presumed authorized duration of stay.
If we can presume that the authorized period of stay is 6 months and that the person can re-enter Canada through the US without applying for a new TRV or Visitor Record, then why does CIC state on another website page the following:
If your visa is still valid and you are travelling only and directly to the United States (including its Territories and Possessions) or St. Pierre and Miquelon, you do not need a new visitor visa to return to Canada. If your visa expires before returníng to Canada from one of these areas, and you are not in possession of a valid visitor record, work permit study permit, or temporary resident permit (authorizing re-entry), you will need to get a new visitor visa.
The above would imply that in order to re-enter Canada through the US on an expired TRV, a foreign national must possess a valid status document (visitor record, study permit, work permit or TRP) and that they would not be allowed to re-enter on their initial 6 month authorized period of stay.
Thank you for taking the time to clarify this information and responding to my inquiry.
With kind regards
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for reaching out to IRCC on the question of authorized period of stay and traveling to the US or St. Pierre and Miquelon.
According to Regulation R183(2) a FN is authorized to stay in Canada as a temporary resident for a period of 6 months or any other period that is fixed by an officer. According to R183(3)(a) and (c) the period authorized for the stay of a temporary resident begins on the day on which they enter Canada. Furthermore, the program delivery instructions outline that “If you need a visa to enter Canada, the length of your stay will be for six months unless otherwise specified." Additionally, According to IRCC website, if there is no stamp, handwritten date or document in your passport, your temporary resident status will expire six months from the day you arrived in Canada.
Therefore, a FN who needs a TRV to enter Canada, unless otherwise specified by an officer, is authorized to stay for a period of six months which begins on the day they entered Canada.
Additionnaly, according to R190(3)(f)(ii), foreign nationals who are normally required to have TRVs to enter Canada are exempt from that requirement when they seek to re-enter, if, since leaving Canada after being authorized to enter as a temporary resident, they have only visited St. Pierre and Miquelon or the U.S. (including the Territories and Possessions of the U.S., but not including cruises that enter international waters) if they return to Canada by the end of the period initially authorized for their stay or any extension to it.
Therefore, a FN whose initial TRV has expired, is exempt from the requirement of a new TRV when re-entering Canada before the end of their authorized period of stay of 6 months, when the FN only travelled to St Pierre and Miquelon or the US.
We thank you for bringing the issue to our attention. Steps have been undertaken to correct the instructions.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Inbox

Question: This is a question regarding holding a post-graduation work permit and applying for a study permit to study a Master degree (part time or full time)
Student is in his last term (W2016) Student will be eligible for PGWP as of May 20th once the official mark is posted

threads.subject: Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA). - REP-2016-0185
threads.question:
Hello:
中 and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada My question is in regards to the new Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA).
If an individual received a study or work permit from CBSA at a port of entry on or after August 1, 2015, did he automatically
get issued an ETA by CBSA?
If so, how can this individual verify he actually has an ETA (to be sure before he travels by air on March 15, 2016)?Is the ETA number put on the face of the work permit issued to him? So far, I have not seen any work permits (issued after Aug. 1/15 to persons who need an ETA) which contain an ETA number.
How can an individual check for sure whether or not he has an ETA needed for his travel after March 15, 2016?
The reason for my question is that on the CiC website, there is a reference that states that "Starting August 1, 2015, an ETA will be issued automatically if you were approved for a work or study permit. You will not have to submit a separate ETA
application form or pay a separate fee."See [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/questions-answers-by-topic.asp?](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/questions-answers-by-topic.asp?) st=16.7
However, I spoke with a CiC call-centre agent who specifically told me that an ETA will not be automatically granted to an individual who received a work permit at a port of entry on or after August 1, 2015, but rather the automatic granting of an ETA will commence on or after March 15, 2016.
This information is conflicting and it is important the public knows what it needs to do for travel after March 15, 2016.
As noted above, my question specifically is: If an individual has been issued a work or study permit on or after August 1, 2015 at a port of entry to Canada, were they automatically granted an ETA? How do they know? Is there a way to confirm that an ETA was granted to them and if so, how is that done?
Lastly, and in addition to the foregoing, would accompanying family members who were issued status documents after Aug. 1, 2015 (accompanying the principal applicant at a port of entry) also be granted automatic ETA's? For example, if an individual is granted a work permit after Aug. 1/15, and their spouse is granted an accompanying open work permit and their children receive either study permits or visitor records at a port of entry, would these accompanying family members also have automatically received an ETA?
Thank you
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your enquiries.
Our apologies for the conflicting information you have received. Indeed, a visa-exempt foreign national who was issued a study or work permit at a port of entry on or after August 1, 2015 was also simultaneously issued an eTA. The validity of this eTA is independent from that of the study or work permit; in other words, the eTA is valid for five years (or passport expiry, whichever occurs sooner). An important distinction to make is that the validity of an eTA issued with an initial study or work permit is not simultaneously extended when an application for a study or work permit extension is approved. In these cases, should the foreign national's eTA be nearing its expiration, the foreign national will need to submit an application for a new eTA separately from their study or work permit extension application.
Visa-exempt foreign nationals who apply for and receive a study or work permit at a port of entry do not receive a confirmation letter regarding their permit (or eTA), but are nonetheless given a physical study or work permit counterfoil. We recognize that in not providing the eTA number to visa-exempt study and work permit applicants who apply for and receive a study or work permit at a port of entry, this has created an issue whereby these clients are unable to verify whether they possess a valid eTA, and for how long that eTA is valid. We are therefore exploring the means by which we can regularly and
consistently provide these clients with their eTA number at the port of entry.
In the interim, these clients will need to request their eTA number via our webform. Once received, they may use this number, along with some details from the passport to which their study or work permit is issued, to verify the status of their eTA on our website.
With regards to your question about accompanying family members, yes, accompanying family members who were issued status documents at a port of entry on or after August 1, 2015, should have been automatically issued an eTA. Since accompanying family members would have submitted separate applications for open work permits, the eTAs would be generated with those applications. To obtain their eTA number, these individuals would also need to follow the steps outlined above.
We hope that this clarifies things for you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Inbox

For a student who has graduated from a Canadian post-secondary institution, only work experience gained after graduation will count towards meeting the work experience requirement under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC).
As per the Program Delivery Instructions published on our website as a courtesy to stakeholders, any period of employment during which the applicant was engaged in full-time study will not be included in calculating the period of qualifying work experience under the CEC (e.g., work experience gained through co-op work permits, off-campus work permits while a full-time student and on-campus work permits). This may prove difficult where a significant period of experience on an off-campus work permit is claimed by the applicant prior to changes to the international student program which came into effect June 1, 2014, given that holders were required to voluntarily surrender their off-campus work permit if they were no longer studying on a full-time basis and had therefore become ineligible for the program.

threads.answer:
Dear
Please find below the response to your questions with regards to the difference between Super Visa and the Multiple Entry
Visa:
Question: Does this mean a parent who is issued a 10- year multiple entry "super visa " will be allowed entry to Canada more than once for a period of two years i.e. each time they are allowed entry to Canada pursuant to the 10-year multiple entry visa issued to them, the POE officer will authorize a stay in Canada for a period of two years?
Answer: The Super Visa is a multi-entry visa that provdes multiple entries for a period up to 10 years. The key difference is that the Super Visa allows an individual to stay for up to two years_on initial entry into Canada, while a 10-year multiple entry visa would have a status period for each entry of only six months. Please refer to: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?) gnum=426&top=16

Answer: There is no guarantee that the client would be granted a second two-year authorized stay upon re-entry with a multiple-entry Super Visa that is still valid. As mentioned earlier, the key difference is that the Super Visa allows an individual to stay for up to two years on initial entry into Canada.
Question: What about parents from a visa exempt country who have applied at a visa office or online for entry under the super visa program? Will the letter of introduction provided to such parents by the visa office allow them multiple entries to Canada, each of which such multiple entries will be authorized by the POE officer to be for a duration of two years?
Answer: As with foreign nationals from visa-required countries, there is no guarantee that the visa-exempt client would be granted a second two-year authorized stay upon re-entry with a multiple-entry letter of introduction that is still valid. As mentioned earlier, the key difference is that the Super Visa allows an individual to stay for up to two years on initial entry into Canada.
Please note that starting March 15, 2016, visa-exempt foreign nationals who fly to or transit through Canada will need an Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA). Exceptions include U.S. citizens and travelers with a valid visa. Visa-exempt Super Visa applicants will have to apply separately for an eTA after they receive their Super Visa letter of introduction from the visa office.

threads.subject: Canadian Work Experience under Express Entry-REP-2016-0275
threads.question:
Dear Sirs/Mesdames:
I am wondering whether there are any circumstances in which a period of self-employment can be counted as Canadian work experience to gain points under Express Entry. I believe the situation I am dealing with represents a serious flaw in the Express Entry points calculation system. My client is in his early 30s, he completed a doctorate at the University of British Columbia, and he has worked in Canada approximately 30 hours per week since he graduated in 2011. However, he is a musician and the nature of that industry is that he enters into contractor relationships with his employers instead of employment relationships. He has a list of engagements and work experience that is five pages long, including extensive work with the Prince George Symphony Orchestra as well as other orchestras. He is a very talented trumpet player and teaches music in addition to being a performance artist.
This type of contribution to Canadian culture should be recognized under Express Entry, but due to the fact that musicians are almost always contractors, he receives no points for previous Canadian work experience and with only 419 points he does not seem close to receiving an invitation to apply for permanent residence. His temporary resident status is set to expire soon, and we are in danger of losing this talented musician to the United States.
My question is, are there any plans to either (1) recognize significant cultural contributions under Express Entry, or (2) allow musicians and other performance artists to claim self-employed work for Canadian work experience?
Sincerely,
Page 371
is withheld pursuant to section est retenue en vertu de l'article
of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
threads.answer:
Good day,
As per paragraph 15(7)(b) of the Ministerial Instructions Respecting the Express Entry System, and without exception, periods of self-employment do not count for purposes of points for 'Canadian work experience' under the Comprehensive Ranking System.
Foreign nationals with relevant experience in a range of jobs generally considered part of Canada's artistic and cultural fields, including musicians and performing artists, may be eligible to apply for permanent residence under the Self-Employed Persons Class.

Express Entry: determining if an e-APR has passed the completeness check
If a foreign national submits an APR using Express Entry, they may apply for a BOWP if they meet the eligibility requirements. However, a decision on the application will not be made until the Centralized Intake Office (ClO) has assessed the e--APR for completeness. A BOWP can be issued only if the e--APR has passed the R10 completeness check.

Incomplete application: The CIO will cancel the e--APR and enter the following note in GCMS: “E--APR rejected as incomplete. Client not eligible for BOWP."

threads.answer:

threads.subject: Adoption of child from a country (specifically Iran) where the Hague Convention is not in force-REP-2016- 0052
threads.question:
Dear Sir or Madam,
My questions are in reference to the adoption of child from a country (specifically Iran) where the Hague Convention is not in force.
1. If the adopted parents who are Canadian Citizens decide to pursue the citizenship process will they require a no objection letter from the their habitual province of residence in Canada?
2. If the adopted parents who are Canadian Citizens decide to pursue the immigration process will they require a no objection letter from the their habitual province of residence in Canada?
3. What is the processing time for both the citizenship process and the immigration process?
4. How will the process (either the citizenship or immigration process) be complicated if the country where the adoption is taking place gives a legal guardianship of child instead of adoption order?
5. If possible, can you please specify IRCC's requirements (such as required documents etc.) for adoption and the complete steps which need to be taken in both Canada and Iran which will allow a smooth process in bring the child to Canada?
I look forward to hearing from you.
Thank you and best regards,
Page 11

threads.answer:
Dear Sir,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox
Intercountry adoption is a complex issue, given the need to comply with the laws of States of origin as well as Receiving Štates (in Canada, federal, provincial and territorial legislation).
The Hague Convention: The Hague Convention on Protection of Children and Co-operation in Respect of Intercountry Adoption (Hague Convention), to which Canada is Party, only recognizes adoptions that create a permanent parent-child relationship between the adoptive parents and their adopted child (Article 2(1)). In legal terms, the adopted child enjoys all the same rights as those of a biological child in the same family.
The State of origin Law: According to the Iranian Government, guardianship exists in the Iranian Law, but not adoption. In any case, only applicants residing in Iran can apply for guardianship. Also, “adoption"is accepted in the Islamic Republic of Iran under the title of guardianship. Children may be put under the tutorship and supervision of a competent family by a judicial decree and in accordance with the Act Concerning Protection of Children Without Parents. Article 1 of this Act provides that "every wife and husband residing in Iran can take care of a child upon mutual agreement and in accordance with approval of the court and pursuant to the regulations and relating to child supervision (adoption)". Thus, applicants residing outside Iran cannot apply for "adoption". Prospective adoptive guardians must reside in Iran and must comply with the six month probationary period.
The legal regimes (adoption vs kafala): The legal concept of kafala under Islamic Law (which provides for the substitute care of a minor who cannot be cared for by his / her family and does not affect the original parent-child relationship or create a new parent-child relationship with the person under who care the child is entrusted); distinguishes it from the western legal understanding of adoption which creates a new, permanent parent-child relationship.
The IRPA/IRPR Legislation: The Immigration & Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and its Regulations (IRPR) require that an immigration officer be satisfied that a child to be adopted is "legally available in that country for adoption." "Adoptions" from countries governed in whole, or in part, by Islamic law (i.e. Islamic countries) are not consistent with IRPA and its regulations, or specific international instruments (Hague Convention) involving children,
The Provinces/Territories responsibilities for adoption: In Canada, the process to adopt a child falls under the responsibility of the provinces and territories. Provincial and Territorial central authorities evaluate prospective adoptive parents regarding their suitability to adopt and assist them directly with the adoption process. In the case of intercountry adoption, your first contact should be the provincial or territorial central adoption authority in the province or territory where you reside. Please consult the following link to find the list of provincial and territorial adoption central authorities in Canada:
[http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/immigrate/adoption/authorities.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/immigrate/adoption/authorities.asp)
The province or territory to which the child is destined may provide a written statement that they do not object to the adoption for both an adoption via the citizenship or immigration process.
Once an adoption is complete, the (IRCC) is responsible for facilitating status and entry to Canada. Two streams are available for adoptive parents: the immigration process via sponsorship in the family pursuant to the Immigration and Refugees Protection Act and Immigration and Refugees Protection Regulations, and the citizenship process via the Citizenship Act.
For additional information, please consult the following links: Choose a process—Intercountry adoption: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/immigrate/adoption/differences.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/immigrate/adoption/differences.asp)

threads.answer:
Dear Madam,
Thank-you for your query. We apologize for the delayed response.
To answer your first question, a sponsor who signed an engagement with the province of Quebec and subsequently moves from Quebec to another province while their sponsorship application is in process must complete and submit a new IMM 1344 Application to Sponsor, Sponsorship Agreement and Undertaking to the Case Processing Centre in Mississauga. This is because Quebec has sole authority for assessing sponsorship eligibility in cases where the applicant will be residing in that province. When a sponsor and applicant move to another province, the sponsor's eligibility must be assessed to ensure they meet federal requirements.

threads.answer:
Good day,
Question:
Would a person applying for an inland common-law sponsorship and work permit be considered to have implied status once the lEC work permit expires if the application for spons orship and work permit is submitted before the expiry date of the lEC work permit?
Response: The implied status provision R183(5) applies to foreign nationals who submit their application for a work permit extension to prior to the expiry of their present status. The application for extension of their work permit under R201 allows for the temporary resident to continue working without a permit under R186(u), this provision may not apply to lEC participants as they are generally submitting their work permit applications under A30 and therefore do not benefit from implied status or authorization to work without a permit.
Under International Experience Canada Program, foreign nationals are subject to terms and conditions of their countries'bilateral agreement/arrangement with Canada. As a rule, participants under lEC cannot renew or extend their work permit application under lEC Program. As some countries allow participation in the Program more than once, applicants have to apply for a new participation and a new work permit outside of Canada (i.e., under A30).
In some limited circumstances, implied status provision may apply to certain IEC participants. For example, if the foreign national had an offer of employment of 24 months validity period under the Working Holidays stream but they were issued a work permit for a lesser duration due to an administrative error or to match the validity period of the foreign national's passport. If the foreign national wishes to continue working with the same employer under the same conditions as their previous work permit to reach the maximum validity period allowed (24 months), then he/she may submit an application to extend the work permit to reach the maximum period allowed (24 months). In such cases, if they applied before their work permit expires, they may still have implied status until the decision is made on their application.

Immigration Representatives Inbox

threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your enquiry. Apologies for the delay in responding. As we are unable to respond to case specific questions, please find below some general information in response to your questions.
Responses to questions 1 and 2: Under Express Entry, all applicants for permanent residence and their family members 18 and older must include in their application, police certificates for each country or territory where they have lived for six or more months in total since the age of 18. In some countries, it can take a long time to get police certificates. If applicants did not start the process to get the police certificates before the invitation to apply (ITA), they should do this right away in order to submit them before the 60 days are up.
In some cases, applicants may not be able to get a police certificate despite their best efforts. (For example, if they applied in the first week after they were invited to apply, but it did not arrive within the 60 day timeframe.) If this happens, applicants should upload proof that they applied for the document (such as a receipt that proves that they submitted paperwork and any fees to request the document) and a letter of explanation. Applicants must show that they made their best efforts to get the document.
There is no guarantee that IRCC will accept a letter of explanation in place of a police certificate. IRCC considers each application on its own merits. Someone who is working in Canada on an LMlA-based work permit is able to claim the additional 600 Comprehensive Ranking System points for arranged employment provided they have a job offer letter from their current employer indicating that they are being offered continuous, paid, full-time work in a skilled occupation on a permanent/indeterminate basis.
