threads.answer:
Good day,
This is in response to your enquiry submitted to the Immigration Representatives mailbox on February 15, 2016.
Question:
Would you please let me know if, and if so on which conditions, New Zealand nationals can extend or renew their lEC WHP work permits, if they were issued a one-year IEC WHP work permit on or after 2 April 2015? I refer to the information provided here: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/work/iec/eligibility.asp?country=nz&cat=wh](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/work/iec/eligibility.asp?country=nz&cat=wh)
- Do I understand correctly that, depending on the point in time applicants participated in the program, they may still benefit from the additional 11 months?
- If so, what moment in time does "participated in lEC before April 2, 2015" signify? Is it the work permit issuance date on arrival in Canada, or is it the date of the work permit approval (PoE Introduction) letter prior to this?
- If a New Zealand participant is eligible to apply for the additional 11 months, would they be able to apply for the extension to CPC Vegreville?
Response:
There are limited circumstances under which New Zealand nationals can extend or renew their IEC WHP work permits if they were issued a one-year IEC WHP work permit on or after April 2, 2015. For example, an applicant who submitted their application after April 2, 2015, but received a work permit valid for only 12 months due to an administrative error may be eligible to extend their work permit to receive the remaining 11 months. To do so, applicants must complete the in-Canada Case Specific Enquiry web form and send it to IRCC by choosing “International Experience Canada (other countries)" under “Type of application”. The lEC participant will need to provide, via the web form, a justification for requesting the extension. However, applicants who were issued a 12-month work permit because they did not satisfy program requirements (i.e. their Health Insurance was valid for only 12 months) will not be able to extend their work permit. They may be able to apply for a new work permit outside of IEC program. If they apply for a new work permit under another program (LMIA required or LMIA exempt), they must apply at least 30 days before their IEC work permit expires.
If the client applied for and was issued a Letter of Introduction (LOl) under International Experience Canada Program and came to Canada before April 2, 2015, then they are only entitled to the length of their work permit issued to them by the Canada Border Services Agency at the port of entry (POE). This also applies to those who applied prior to April
2nd, 2015 but whose work permit was issued at the POE after that date.
Under administrative law, a client who was given a letter of introduction and issued a work permit under a previously agreed to bilateral agreement cannot benefit from the new terms and conditions of the renegotiated bilateral agreement that extends the participation period up with their country.
Applicants who were either a) currently participating when the new agreement between Canada and New Zealand
Lon came into effect or b) had received a letter of introduction under the 2014 year but activated their work permit after April 2nd 2015 are not eligible to receive the 23-month participation, nor are they eligible to extend their work permits.
Regards,

threads.subject: Work Permit and Childcare-REP-2016-0239
threads.question:
Hello,
If there is no condition listed on a worker's work permit prohibiting them from working with childcare, are they permitted to do so. Would this still be the case even if the worker did not complete a medical examination before obtaining that work permit?
If they are unable to work without first completing a medical, how would a worker then get a condition that is not on their work permit changed to permit them to work in childcare?
Thank-you.
Best Regards,
and Cizenship Caneda
threads.answer:
Good day,
QUESTION 1: If there is no condition listed on a worker's work permit prohibiting them from working with childcare, are they permitted to do so. Would this still be the case even if the worker did not complete a medical examination before obtaining that work permit?
RESPONSE 1: A work permit generally lists a specific occupation and a specific employer. If a temporary resident holds an open work permit then they can work for any employer in any occupation without an Immigration Medical examination except a designated occupation. Childcare is considered a designated occupation -please see Medical exam requirements for temporary residents -Jobs for which you need a medical exam for further instructions on how to obtain an immigration medical examination.
QUESTION 2: If they are unable to work without first completing a medical, how would a worker then get a condition that is not on their work permit changed to permit them to work in childcare?
RESPONSE 2: Subparagraph 30(1)(a)(ii) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations requires foreign nationals intending to work in a designated occupation to submit to a medical exam. If the foreign national wants to work in child care they must take and pass a medical examination and then apply to change the conditions of their work permit. Even though the condition may not be specifically listed on the work permit, if the foreign national knows they have not completed a medical examination they would be in violation of the Regulations to work in childcare without a medical examination. The foreign national would add the information that they wish to work in childcare but had not previously completed their medical examination.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Inbox

threads.subject: Provincial misrepresentation-REP-2016-0362
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madame:
We have a question regarding the effect of a finding of misrepresentation by a provincial nominee program in an application under that program. The importance of this issue arises as many provincial programs (e.g. Manitoba) have a 2 year bar on re- application after a finding of misrepresentation. However, IRPA s. 40 has a 5 year bar. Our question therefore is whether a finding of misrepresentation made by a province leads only to the 2 year bar under that province's rules; or whether that finding is then grounds for a 5 year bar from immigration to Canada under the Act.
Please let me know if you would like me to clarify the question. Thank you greatly for your time and consideration.
Regards,
Page 235
is withheld pursuant to section est retenue en vertu de l'article
of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
中 and Citizenship Caneda
threads.answer:
Dearimmigration representative,
When applicants apply under a Provincial Nominee Program (PNP), they are first assessed by that province/territory to
determine whether the applicant meets the jurisdictional requirements for that program. If the province/territory
determines that the applicant does meet the criteria, the applicant may be nominated and advised to apply to , (IRCC) for permanent residence. If the province/territory determines that the applicant does not meet the program criteria, the applicant may be refused by that jurisdiction. In situations where an applicant has misrepresented themselves in their application, provincial/territorial authorities may ban the applicant from re-applying to their program. This measure, including the length of such as ban, is set by provincial/territorial policy or legislation. Not all jurisdictions have policies or legislation regarding banning for misrepresentation.
If, however, misrepresentation is identified at the federal level (e.g., when someone applies for permanent residence after being nominated), the foreign national can be found inadmissible for misrepresentation under s.40 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). A foreign national who is inadmissible under this section continues to be inadmissible for
misrepresentation for five years and, during that time, may not apply for permanent resident status.
As such, applications that are processed at the provincial/territorial level are subject to provincial/territorial policies and legislation, until successful candidates are referred to IRCC. Keep in mind that, if provincial/territorial authorities have reason to believe that an individual may be contravening IRPA (e.g., staying in Canada past the validity of their visa, working without a visa, producing fraudulent documents, etc.), they may refer the information to the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) for investigation and/or enforcement action, and any findings of misrepresentation may result in a 5-year ban under IRPA.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Inbox

threads.subject: INQUIRY ON AGE CUT OFF FOR IEC GRET BRITAIN-REP-2016-0314
threads.question:
1*1and Cizenship Canada
Hi Team,
I am trying to do an eligibility assessment for Working Holiday lEC. My only conclusion for the refusal is that The person I am doing it for is from Britain and turns 31 on July 10, 2016. Might that be a refusal reason for finding one ineligible? What is the cut off time for some one who applies at 30 years of age?
Kindly advise.
中 and Citizenship Caneda
threads.answer:
Hello
Thank you for email to the Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question: I am trying to do an eligibility assessment for Working Holiday lEC. My only conclusion for the refusal is that The person I am doing it for is from Britain and turns 31 on July 10, 2016. Might that be a refusal reason for finding one ineligible? What is the cut off time for some one who applies at 30 years of age?
Response:
While we cannot provide case-specific guidance, we will provide general guidance that may inform your course of action.
As long as the letter of Introduction is valid, persons in the scenarios you described are not affected if they turn 31 years old within its validity period (one year from the date of issue). In the case of UK where the cutoff age is 30, it does not matter if an applicant is 31 by the time his application is processed as long as the work permit application was submitted when the applicant was 30. International Experience Canada (IEC) approved work permit applications receive Letters of Introduction (LOI) valid for 12 months after their approval.
Upon presentation of a valid LOl at a Canadian port of entry, a work permit is issued and is not to be affected by the age of the participant, as long as the age when the work permit application was submitted is eligible. For example, there could be a situation where a UK citizen submitted a work permit application when he was 30, then was 31 when approved and came to Canada 12 months later at 32 for a work permit valid for 24 months, i.e. valid until the person is 34 years old.
IEC refusals
Officers make decisions on a case-by-case basis, as you may know there is no formal appeal process if a temporary resident visa is refused. However, if a foreign national's work permit application was refused and they would still like to participate in IEC, they will need to create a new profile. Depending on the situation, they may be eligible for one or more lEC categories. Should they submit a new profile and enter a pool, a new work permit application will be needed when an Invitation to Apply (ITA) is received. Only candidates invited from a pool can apply for a work permit under lEC.
Trusting this information is of assistance.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Inbox

threads.subject: [cbancism] Settlement funds for a PR applicant on a post-grad work permit currently employed-REP-20I6-0391
threads.question:
Dear Immreps,
A colleague forwarded the e-mail below on the settlement funds requirements for r.205(a) work permit holders. I understand that IRCC has made a policy decision not to require settlement funds for applicants who have r.205(a) work permits.
I have similar questions about r.204 PNP work permit holders:
1. In order to create a profile in the Express Entry system, one has to qualify in either FSW or CEC, both of which require settlement funds-even if the intention is to apply in the PNP class. However, there is no verification at the profile stage. Do you require applicants to have proof of settlement funds at the profile creation stage? Would an applicant who intends to apply through Express Entry in the PNP class be able to create an Express Entry profile if they indicated no settlement funds available at the profile creation stage?
2. Assuming an applicant has created a profile and received PNP Express Entry Nomination, has been invited to apply for PR in the PNP class and has done so and been approved, do you require proof of settlement funds at the landing stage? Would it make a difference if their work permit was issued under r.204 pursuant to their nomination, vs. some other type of non-r.203 work permit?
Thank you,
threads.answer:
Dear Sir,
All candidates completing an Express Entry profile are required to answer the question regarding available settlement funds as this information may become relevant depending on the candidate's circumstances, and the specific program under which they may be invited to apply should they be deemed eligible for the Express Entry pool.
A candidate should indicate the total amount of money available at the time they complete their Express Entry profile. If invited to apply as a candidate currently authorized to work in Canada with a valid offer of arranged employment, then the individual would be exempt from the requirement to include proof of settlement funds with their application for permanent residence.
For those who require settlement funds, proof of settlement funds will be required as part of a complete application. To confirm whether the applicant meets the low-income cut-off (LICO), assessed by the amount of money they hold, compared to the number of people in their family, requires that the applicant include all supporting documentation to validate information contained in their Express Entry profile and their e-APR.
We understand the issue of whether or not settlement funds are required can seem complicated. Consequently we have tried to simplify the issue by providing you with an overview of the various scenarios below. Please keep in mind that CEC applicants are not required to provide proof of settlement funds in their eAPR. Other exemptions granted within programs are based on the type of work permit issued. So, for example, if an applicant applies under the PNP program, the exemption would be granted depending on whether or not they meet MEC for either FSW, FSTP or CEC and on the type of work permit issued.
Under the Federal Skilled Worker Program (FSWP) and the Federal Skilled Trades Program (FSTP), all applicants must meet the settlement funds requirement, with the exception of applicants who meet one of the following scenarios:
Scenario Notes Applicant is currently working in Canada on a work permit that was issued based on a positive Labour Market 1 See Note 1 Impact Assessment (LMIA) and has a valid job offer from an employer in Canada. Applicant is currently working in Canada on an LMlA-exempt work permit that was issued in accordance with 2 See Note 2 paragraph R204(a) or R204(c) and has a job offer (with or without an LMIA) from an employer in Canada. Applicant is currently working in Canada as an intra-company transferee (ICT) under the General Agreement 3on Trade in Services (GATS) on a LMIA-exempt work permit that was issued in accordance with paragraph See Note 3 R205(a) and has a job offer (with or without an LMIA) from an employer in Canada.
Note 1: The requirements for a job offer to be considered valid are slightly different according to the program. Under the FSwP, a job offer is considered to be valid if it is for continuous, paid, full-time work that is permanent, non-seasonal and in Skill Type 0 or Skill Levels A or B of the 2011 National Occupational Classification (NOC) matrix, and if it meets one of the following two conditions:
•The employer making the job offer has a positive LMIA, or The applicant is currently working in Canada in a NOC O, A or B job on a work permit that was issued based on a LMlA; is working for the employer listed on the work permit; is authorized to work in Canada when submitting their application and when the visa is issued; and the employer has made the applicant a full-time job offer if accepted as a permanent resident.
While under the FSTP, a job offer is considered to be valid if it is made by up to two employers, for continuous, paid, full-time work that is for at least one year in a skilled trade occupation (job that starts with 72, 73, 82, 92 or 632 and 633 in the 2011 National Occupational Classification (NOC) matrix), and if it meets one of the following two conditions:
- The employer making the job offer has a positive LMIA, or The applicant is currently working in Canada in a skilled trade job on a work permit that was issued based on a LMlA; is working for an employer listed on the work permit; is authorized to work in Canada when submitting their application and when the visa is issued; and the employer has made the applicant a full-time job offer if accepted as a permanent resident in a job that is in the same three digit level of the NOC as the current job.
Note 2: Even though the applicant's work permit is LMlA-exempt and the employer does not have an LMIA for the job offer, the Regulations
Citoyenneté Canada
exempt the applicant from the settlement funds requirement. Under the FSWP, the applicant meets the definition of arranged employment as defined under R82(2)(b) and therefore does not need settlement funds as per R76(1)(b)(ii). While under the FSTP, the applicant meets the requirement under R87.2(3)(d)(iii) and is consequently exempted as per R87.2(5).
Note 3: Even though the applicant's work permit is LMlA-exempt and the employer does not have an LMIA for the job offer, the Department has made a policy decision to treat ICTs who are working on an LMIA-exempt work permit under GATS in the same way as NAFTA ICTs, whose work permits are issued under R204(a) and thus benefit from the settlement funds exemption (as per Note 2).
I hope this explanation helps clarify the requirements and the exemptions.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

[mailto: ]
Dear
Thank you for your email correspondence to Citizenship and Immigration Canada's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Your client does not need to meet the settlement funds requirement, as he is currently authorized to work in Canada and has a job offer from an employer in Canada. As mentioned in our original response, this also includes those who have a job offer and who are working in Canada as an intra-company transferee (ICT) under the General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS) on a LMIA-exempt work permit. Even though the definition of arranged employment in section 82 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations only refers to work permits issued in accordance with paragraph 204(a) or (c), CIC has made a policy decision to include those issued under paragraph 205(a) for ICTs under GATS.
Please keep in mind that when settlement funds are required, they must be accessible from the time that the application for permanent residence is submitted up until the time that the applicant is granted permanent residence status.
It is also important to mention that in order to obtain additional points under Express Entry for arranged employment, individuals who are currently working in Canada on a LMlA-exempt work permit must have a valid job offer, which is supported by a LMIA.
We hope this information will assist you.
Sincerely,

Question I have a few questions related to the recent changes to Employer Compliance, specifically the form and what the necessary steps are to contact CIC if changes are made to a TFW's position on a LMIA-exempt work permit:
If an employer has hired a TFW based on a LMIA-exempt work permit (eg. NAFTA) and they have completed the Employer Compliance Fee and filled out the form via the Employer Portal and the TFW gets a work permit for three years, what actions would the employer take in the following instances:

Thank you for your question.
If an employer promotes a foreign worker to a higher level position who currently has a valid work permit and who is also exempted from a LMIA, then it is necessary to obtain a new work permit with the new job offer. The employer must use the Employer Portal and also pay the Employer Compliance Fee once again as it is considered to be a new application.

IRCC does not require proactive notification of changes that are part of the regulatory imposed conditions on the employer, such as wages, working conditions, location, etc.

threads.answer:

As you may be aware, applicants must have at least 12 months of full-time, Canadian skilled work experience (or the equivalent in part-time work experience) in one or more NOC 0, A or B occupations within the 36 months before the date of application receipt.

threads.subject: ITA received for FSW, when work experience may not be 'continuous'- REP-2016-0316 - Due by 25 Mar
threads.question:
This is a policy question, not a case specific inquiry. My policy questions are as follows:
1. Do the words ‘in the same job' in your website's description of 'skilled work experience'mean 'for the same employer’ or ‘in the same NOC code'?
2. Where an applicant has amassed 1560 hours of work experience, in the same job (same NOC code, same job title, same job description) but for different employers (working part time for several employers, with hours adding up to full-time), is this ‘continuous' work experience?
3. If this is not continuous work experience, and the applicant was selected for the FSWP, how can an ITA be amended for a CEC selection instead of FSWP?
threads.answer:
Thank you for your inquiry.
The reference on our website to 'in the same job' in the description of qualifying 'skilled work experience' under the Federal Skilled Worker Program (FSWP) means experience in the occupation declared by the candidate/applicant as their primary occupation (i.e. single NOC code).
Consistent with paragraph 75(2)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, a candidate invited to apply under the FSwP must demonstrate at least one year of continuous, qualifying work experience in the single occupation they choose to identify as their primary occupation. There is no requirement that such experience be acquired with a single employer.

criteria.

The onus is on the applicant to demonstrate that the work experience they have claimed was paid. There are no set requirements with respect to frequency of payment.
Students may receive employment income for income tax purposes in different forms, including remuneration reported as "other income” in a T4A slip (e.g. periodic taxable stipends through research grants, assistantships, fellowships). Proof of income derived through such sources would be acceptable for FSW purposes.

threads.subject: Express Entry-LMIA and Bridging work permits-REP-2016-0300
threads.answer:
Mr.
Under section 11.2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act an applicant must demonstrate that the they met the minimum entry criteria for Express Entry and possessed the qualifications for which they were awarded CRS points both at the time they were issued an Invitation to Apply and at the time their electronic application for permanent residence is received by CIC.
Candidates who declare in their Express Entry profile that they have a valid job offer, supported by an LMlA in a skilled occupation will automatically receive an additional 600 points towards their CRS score. If invited to apply, to remain eligible for the 600 points for such a declared valid job offer, a candidate's LMlA-based work permit must continue to be valid when he/she submits her application for permanent residence (e-APR) or he/she must have applied for an LMIA-backed work permit extension before the expiry date of their previous LMlA-backed work permit, and therefore have implied status to continue working for the same employer under the same conditions.
In addition, an applicant is eligible to apply for a BOwP (i.e. currently working in Canada on a work permit due to expire within 4 months) and may submit an application for an open work permit to CPC-Vegreville after submitting their Express Entry e-APR. The Acknowledgment of receipt-Application for permanent residence letter, which is automatically issued to applicants through their MyCIC account, must be submitted along with the BOWP application. Applicants will not lose any points for arranged employment after they are issued a BOWP as long as their original LMIA-backed work permit was valid on the day that their application for permanent residence was submitted.
Please note that before a BOWP can be issued, the applicant's e-APR must first pass the completeness check in accordance with section 10 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. Officers at CPC-Vegreville will check our processing system to ensure that the eAPR is complete before issuing a BOWP. If an e-APR is found to be incomplete and therefore rejected, the applicant is no longer eligible for a BOwP. In these cases, the application for a BOWP will be refused.
We hope this information will assist you. Thank you for your interest in Express Entry.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Inbox

threads.question:
Our client has a Bachelor's degree in Nursing, which was said to be equivalent to an Entry to Practice Professional Degree (135
points for education), as confirmed by your previous email (please see attached).
However, our client's Express Entry points have been incorrectly calculated. Although she has as a Professional Degree, she
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
does not have "two or more certificates, diplomas, or degrees." However her points are calculated as if she had two separate post-secondary degrees.
As a result, she has received 470 points, instead of 458 points.
Is there a policy in which a person who has a professional degree is considered to have "two or more certificates, diplomas or degrees" and therefore the equivalent points for Express Entry? If that is the case, my client has recently received an Invitation to Apply for points at 470, should she accept the Invitation to Apply?
If not, is there a way to correct the number of points for her Express Entry?

Citoenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Thank you for your inquiry.
Our records indicate that your original question was as follows:
"I am a lawyer looking to confirm a procedure regarding Express Entry. A client of mine received her Bachelor of
Nursing and shortly thereafter became a Registered Nurse.
Is her education level:
1) Bachelor degree - 120 CRS points; or is it 2) Professional degree needed to practice in a licensed profession - 135 points Please confirm which level of education should be selected in situations like the above."
Unfortunately, our response to your original query was incorrect. A candidate who has a Canadian educational credential at the bachelor's level in nursing is not entitled to CRS points for a "professional degree" as nursing is not one of the recognized licensed occupations. You note that the candidate does not have two distinct post-secondary credentials. As such, she would be eligible for 120 core CRS points for her Canadian bachelor's degree (with a spouse/common-law partner), and not the 135 points for a professional degree.
In these circumstances, the candidate should re-calculate their score to reflect 'Bachelor's degree' as their highest level of completed education before applying online for permanent residence. If their recalculated score is less than the lowest score in their round of invitations for an Invitation to Apply, they should decline the invitation.

threads.answer:
Dear
The requirements for a qualifying offer of arranged employment differ between the Ministerial Instructions Respecting the Express Entry System (Mis) and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.
As specified in the Mis and noted on our website, where a candidate requires an offer of arranged employment to meet the minimum entry criteria (MEC) under the Federal Skilled Worker Program (FSWP) or Federal Skilled Trades Program (FSTP), or wishes to claim the additional 600 Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points for arranged employment, the offer of employment must be supported by a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) in all cases.
To answer your specific questions:
1. Someone working in Canada under a work permit issued in an LMIA-exempt category such as an intra-company transferee (R205–C12, including GATS) would not be eligible for CRS arranged employment points unless the employer making them a job offer had obtained an LMIA in respect of that offer. However, should such a candidate receive an Invitation to Apply under the FSWP, they may be eligible to receive points for arranged employment against the skilled worker selection grid. Should their electronic application for permanent residence be assessed as complete and should they pass the 11.2 assessment stage, an applicant would be eligible for up to 10 points for arranged employment and 5 points for adaptability when assessed against FSWP selection criteria, provided they had included evidence of a job offer from their current employer with their application and otherwise met the requirements of paragraph R82(2)(b) of the Regulations. For more details about the requirements to be eligible for arranged employment points under FSWP selection criteria, refer to the Program Delivery Instructions published on our website as a courtesy to stakeholders.
2. Only individuals who are currently authorized to work in Canada and who also have a valid job offer from an employer in Canada are exempted from having to demonstrate that they meet the settlement funds requirements in accordance with the regulatory requirements for the FSWP and FSTP. For purposes of assessing the settlement funds requirement, a valid job offer may be defined as per the Regulations or as per the Mls. This means that an individual who is currently working in Canada on an LMiA-exempt work permit does not need to meet the settlement funds requirement if the valid job offer is LMIA-exempt as per the Regulations. In such cases, the individual should upload a letter in the space for Proof of Means of Financial Support in the Document Checklist explaining that they are exempted from meeting the settlement funds requirement per the Regulations. Best regards, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
If an individual holds a study permit, went on the regular summer holidays, and then for health reasons was not able to return to school in September and therefore received a semester off from their studies which was approved by the university. threads.answer:
Good morning,
Question If an individual holds a study permit, went on the regular summer holidays, and then for health reasons was not able to return to school in September and therefore received a semester off from their studies which was approved by the university. Are they still in compliance with their study permit or will their permit become void? Is the individual able to continue studying the following semester on the same study permit? What if the student took one semester off for health reasons (i.e. the January-April semester) and was returning to school for the Summer semester (i.e. May-August)? Is their study permit valid throughout the semester off and are they able to continue studying in May?
Response Study permit holders in Canada need to actively pursue their studies in Canada as per R220.1. This means that they must remain enrolled at a designated learning institution (DLl), and make reasonable and timely progress towards completing their program of study. R222(1)(a) indicates that a study permit becomes invalid 90 days after the study program has been completed. The program is considered complete when the student receives a notification of program completion from the school. Students who have obtained formal approval from their designated learning institution (DLI) to be temporarily absent from the institution will be reported as being on authorized leave by their DLi during the compliance reporting round. In the course of an examination or application, the student's situation and individual circumstances will be assessed on a case by case basis to determine whether they are in compliance with their study permit conditions.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Inbox

and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
Dear Sir/Madam,
According to R199(e), a client who is in Canada with a visitor visa, accompanying his spouse who has a study permit, is allowed to apply for a work permit AFTER entry.
My question is, when his spouse applies for her study permit extension and he applies for his open work permit, does he need to leave the country to change status from visitor to worker, or does CIC send him his open work permit in the mail together with her study permit extension? Does he also get a worker's TRV, or just a permit?

threads.answer:
Dear
Question:
According to R199(e), a client who is in Canada with a visitor visa, accompanying his spouse who has a study permit, is allowed to apply for a work permit AFTER entry.
My question is, when his spouse applies for her study permit extension and he applies for his open work permit, does he need to leave the country to change status from visitor to worker, or does CIC send him his open work permit in the mail together with her study permit extension? Does he also get a worker's TRV, or just a permit?
Answer:
Your client does not need to leave Canada to apply for his work permit. Accompanying spouses or common-law partners of international students are eligible for an open work permit, which means they do not need a job offer or a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) from Service Canada.
However, to seek an open work permit, he will have to include evidence that he is indeed the spouse or common-law partner of a full-time student at a Designated Learning Institution:
- a public post-secondary institution, such as a college, university, or a Collège d’enseignement général et professionnel (CEGEP), in Quebec;
- a private post-secondary institution that operates under the same rules and regulations as a public institution and receives at least 50 percent of its financing for its overall operations from government grants (currently, only private college-level educational institutions in Quebec qualify); or
- a Canadian private institution authorized by provincial statute to confer degrees.
If the work permit is granted, the validity date will coincide with the spouse's study permit.
A TRV is a different document from work permit; it is a visa to travel to Canada, so he would not be issued one if he applies to extend his stay for a work permit as an accompanying spouse or common-law partner.
For more information visit our website: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/study/work-spouse.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/study/work-spouse.asp)
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

中 and Citizenship Caneda

Hello
I am writing to request clarification on whether an applicant in Canada, awaiting their employer specific work permit (based on a positive LMIA), is eligible for the 600 qualifying job offer points under the Express Entry (EE) system. Does your answer change if the LMIA is now expired and was only to support a work permit (not PR and work permit) application? If an employer offers a full-time indeterminate job offer to an applicant are they able to use the expired work permit based LMIA to gain the 600 points under the EE system? There does not appear to be any note about the validity of the LMIA in the MI or IRPR definitions.
Relevant provisions are below:
“qualifying offer of arranged employment” means
(a) an offer of employment, in an occupation listed in Skill Type 0 Management Occupations or Skill Level A or B of the National Occupational Classification matrix, that is made to a foreign national by an employer other than an embassy, high commission or consulate in Canada or an employer that appears on the list referred to in subsection 209.91(3) of the Regulations, for full-time work in Canada that is non-seasonal and indeterminate and that is supported by an opinion referred to in subparagraph 82(2)(c)(ii) of the Regulations that was provided by the Department of Employment and Social Development;
82(2)(c)(ii) an officer has approved the offer of employment based on an assessment — provided to the officer by the Department of Employment and Social Development, on the same basis as an assessment provided for the issuance of a work permit, at the request of the employer or an officer — that the requirements set out in subsection 203(1) with respect to the offer have been met. Thank-you in advance!
Best Regards,
mmigration, Refugees mmigration, Réfugiés
threads.answer:
Dear
Under section 11.2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act an applicant must demonstrate that the they met the minimum entry criteria for Express Entry and possessed the qualifications for which they were awarded CRS points both at the time they were issued an Invitation to Apply and at the time their electronic application for permanent residence is received by CIC.
Candidates who declare in their Express Entry profile that they have a valid job offer, supported by an LMlA in a skilled occupation will automatically receive an additional 600 points towards their CRS score. If invited to apply, to remain eligible for the 600 points for such a declared valid job offer, a candidate's LMiA-based work permit must continue to be valid when he/she submits her application for permanent residence (e-APR) or he/she must have applied for an LMIA-backed work permit extension before the expiry date of their previous LMlA-backed work permit, and therefore have implied status to continue working for the same employer under the same conditions.
In addition, an applicant is eligible to apply for a BOwP (i.e. currently working in Canada on a work permit due to expire within 4 months) and may submit an application for an open work permit to CPC-Vegreville after submitting their Express Entry e-APR. The Acknowledgment of receipt-Application for permanent residence letter, which is automatically issued to applicants through their MyCIC account, must be submitted along with the BOWP application. Applicants will not lose any points for arranged employment after they are issued a BOWP as long as their original LMIA-backed work permit was valid on the day that their application for permanent residence was submitted.
Please note that before a BOWP can be issued, the applicant's e-APR must first pass the completeness check in accordance with section 10 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. Officers at CPC-Vegreville will check our processing system to ensure that the eAPR is complete before issuing a BOWP. If an e-APR is found to be incomplete and therefore rejected, the applicant is no longer eligible for a BOwP. In these cases, the application for a BOwP will be refused.
We hope this information will assist you. Thank you for your interest in Express Entry.

threads.answer:
Thank you for your enquiry.
To maintain their status as a permanent resident, a person must live in Canada for at least two years within a five-year period. A person may count the days spent outside of Canada if their circumstances meet the criteria set out in section 28(2)(a)(ii)(iii) (iv) or (v) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and section 61 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR)
One such circumstance is where a permanent resident was employed outside of Canada. They may count this time towards the two years if during this time: they were an employee of, or under contract to, a Canadian business or the public service of Canada or of a province or territory and as a term of the employment or contract, they were assigned on a full-time basis to:
o a position outside Canada
an affiliated enterprise outside Canada or a client of the Canadian business or the public service outside Canada; and 0they will continue working for the employer in Canada after the assignment. With regards to the scenario where an employee travels outside of Canada at the request of the Canadian business but is not assigned on a full time basis as a term of the employment or contract to a position outside of Canada, this would not appear to meet the requirements to be counted towards the two years as section 61(3) of IRPR requires that the employee is assigned on a full time basis as a term of the employment or contract to a position outside of Canada; an affiliated enterprise outside of Canada; or a client of the Canadian business or public service of Canada. However, IRCC will consider each application on its own merits with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision.
Please see the IRCC Website for more information: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/applications/guides/5445ETOC.asp#appendixA](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/applications/guides/5445ETOC.asp#appendixA) [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=727&top=10](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?qnum=727&top=10)

threads.subject: Retroactivity of 5 year bar on permanent residence due to misrepresentation-REP-2016-0213
threads.question:
To Whom It May Concern,
My client filed an overseas spousal sponsorship application for his wife that was refused due to misrepresentation. In
2013 wife was found inadmissible to Canada for TWO YEARS pursuant to s. 40(2)(a).
I am aware that the laws have now changed and the period of inadmissibility is now 5 years and not two. Is this 5 year bar retroactive? My client is trying to decide whether to withdraw an lAD appeal now that 2 years have passed and re- sponsor. If the section is retroactive, he would not be able to do so. Your response is greatly appreciated.
Yours very truly,
中 and Citizenship Caneda
threads.answer:
Dear
On November 21, 2014, paragraph 40(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act was amended to change the consequence for misrepresentation from a two-year period of inadmissibility to a five-year period of inadmissibility with a five-year ban on reapplying for permanent residence.
Refusals based on misrepresentation made prior to coming into force of the legislation (November 21, 2014) are subject to the previous legislation (two-year inadmissibility period). As such, if the foreign national was refused based on misrepresentation and found to be inadmissible in 2013, the sponsor would be able to reapply to sponsor the foreign national now, given that that the two-year inadmissibility period has passed.

threads.subject: Dual Intent LMIAs-REP-2016-0459 - Due by 21 Apr
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
I am writing to enquire if there is an obligation on an employer to use both parts of a dual-intent LMiA within the six months of its issuance or if the work permit could be applied for within the six months of its issuance prior to its expiry date and the permanent residence application submitted after that but prior to the expiry of the work permit? So, for example, if a two year work permit is issued pursuant to a dual intent LMlA, would it be acceptable to submit the EE profile after one year when the foreign national qualifies under the CEC.
The indication on the previously approved dual-intent LMIAs that we have received is that the foreign worker must apply for
a work permit or a PR visa prior to the expiry date.
On page one of the LMIA the wording is as follows:
"This LMIA is issued with reference to your stated commitment to:
Support both a work permit application and a permanent residence application (this means the employer will hire the foreign national as a temporary foreign worker before or while the permanent residence application is being processed)."
There is no specific reference anywhere to a requirement to use both parts of the dual intent LMIA prior to its expiry.
Thank you very much for your guidance.
Kind regards,
and Citizenship Caneda
threads.answer:
Thank you for your inquiry.
An LMIA must be used for its intended purpose within the 6-month validity period, or expiry date, as indicated on the LMIA.
An employer who wishes to hire a skilled worker temporarily and make a valid job offer that meets the requirements of one of the three federal immigration programs managed through Express Entry, must apply for an LMlA in support of both a work permit application and a potential application for permanent residence as a skilled immigrant (i.e. a "dual intent" LMiA). In this case, if the employer obtains a positive LMlA, it must be used by the foreign worker to submit an application for an LMIA- based work permit within six months. Assuming their work permit application is approved and they are working in Canada for the employer specified on that work permit at the time they complete their Express Entry profile, the foreign worker would indicate that have a job offer from their current employer in order to obtain additional points for arranged employment towards their Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score. As the "dual intent" LMIA was used within the 6-month validity period for the initial purpose of supporting the candidate's work permit application, it would not also still need to be valid at the time the candidate submits their Express Entry profile or at the point at which an invitation to apply, if any, is issued.
An employer who does not wish to hire a skilled worker temporarily, but rather wishes to make a job offer that meets the requirements of one of the three federal immigration programs managed through Express Entry and hire the worker only if a permanent resident visa is issued, may apply for an LMlA in support of a potential application for permanent residence as a skilled immigrant only (i.e. a "permanent" LMIA). In this case, in order for the candidate to have a valid job offer and be eligible for additional CRS points for arranged employment, the LMIA must be within the 6-month validity period both at the time the candidate submits their Express Entry profile and on the date their application for permanent residence is received, should they be invited to apply.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

As noted on our website, to be considered for the Federal Skilled Worker Program with a foreign education credential or to receive Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points for foreign education for themselves or their spouse or common-law partner, Express Entry candidates must have an Educational Credential Assessment (ECA) report from a designated organization indicating that the foreign educational credential is equivalent to a completed Canadian educational credential. There are no exceptions to this requirement.
The organizations designated to complete Educational Credential Assessment (ECA) reports require that the individual obtain official transcripts from the academic institutions that issued their credential(s). This documentation is required so that the organizations can adequately verify the authenticity of the foreign educational credential(s) and issue a valid ECA report for immigration purposes.
In some circumstances, it may be difficult for an individual to meet the document requirements specified by a designated ECA organization. If possible, it is recommended that the individual submit any other educational credentials they may have received from other countries for purposes of obtaining an ECA report.
Currently, foreign nationals may always submit an ECA application to one of the designated organizations. Evidence of any issues encountered in making arrangements to have official academic records sent directly by the applicable institution(s) should be documented in a letter of explanation included in the ECA application.
While designated organizations will consider such applications, there is no guarantee as to the outcome of their assessment. Documentation submitted as part of the application will need to satisfy the organization's measure of authenticity. Depending on the specific circumstances, the application could be delayed until a means for properly verifying the authenticity of the credentials are established.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

1. The employer making the job offer has a positive PR Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA), or
2. The candidate: is currently working in Canada in a NOC Skill Type O or Skill Level A or B job on a work permit that was issued based on an LMIA (WP or dual intent); is working for an employer listed on the work permit; is authorized to work in Canada when submitting their application and when the visa is issued; and has received a job offer from their employer for a full-time, non-seasonal, indeterminate job in NOC Skill Type O, A or B if accepted as a permanent resident.

However, they may qualify for 'arranged employment' points under the Federal Skilled Worker grid in accordance with paragraph R82(2)(b). threads.question:
Good day,
We are uploading an Expression of Interest (EOl) on behalf of our client who has taken the TEF test. We have confirmed that we are able to combine different portions from different TEF scores, using the highest of each to be eligible for permanent residence. My question is, which of the 3 numbers should I enter in the EOl box where it asks for the test number? Should I put the first one, explain it in my submissions and then upload all 3 or will it be refused
for some reason if I do that?
Please note that we did sent this inquiry to the Express Entry technical issue email but they responded and told us to
forward our inquiry to you.
Thanks
threads.answer:
Dear
You have indicated below that "We have confirmed that we are able to combine different portions from different TEF scores, using the highest of each to be eligible for permanent residence." However, please be advised that this is incorrect, as results of multiple language tests with differing scores by language ability will not be accepted as evidence of meeting the language proficiency requirement for programs managed through Express Entry.
The wording of section 74(7) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations is clear that applicants must submit the results of an evaluation by a designated testing agency demonstrating that they meet or exceed the language proficiency threshold set by the Minister in all four language skill areas. The reference to "an evaluation" in the Regulations means that the results of a single language test must demonstrate that the applicant meets the required language proficiency threshold in all four skill areas.
However, in the case of the Test d'évaluation de français (TEF) where "compulsory" reading and listening comprehension tests may be administered separately from the "optional" written and oral expression tests, IRCC will accept test results from separately administered TEF modules provided they demonstrate the applicant has met or exceeded the applicable language proficiency threshold in all four language abilities, and the test results are less than two years old on the date of application receipt. In this case, there should never be more than two TEF test results.
To address your specific question on which of the test numbers should be entered in the Express Entry system, when the TEF test was taken in two sittings, it is the test with the LATER date (the second, more recent date) that should be inputted. That is the one that will be used to determine when the results expire. Then, an explanation letter should be uploaded to include the number of the second test. It is also recommended that both tests be uploaded as proof up front to avoid the possibility of having to provide them at a later time.
Regards,

The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Question: In this case, credit appears to have been allotted for the month of April, as well as the month of May so as to qualify this individual as a CEC applicant. He is not eligible to be invited as a CEC applicant until May 19, 2016 and he was invited on April 6, 2016. Did the system somehow automatically did calculate excess hours or other entitlement?
Proposed Answer: Our calculation is based off of monthly units, and we do not take into account days. When inputting work experience From and To dates, the system only asks for month and year for each entry. That said, the date range is inclusive, meaning the month in the To date will count towards the calculation of full time equivalent units for that particular work experience entry. Example: Using the May 1st date, and assuming the candidate worked for a year (full-time and met relevant definition of work experience), the calculation would be as follows depending on whether To Date is set to April or May:
May 2015 - April 2016 = 12 months full-time equivalent duration
May 2015 – May 2016 = 13 months full-time equivalent duration
In your case, the "To date" is set to “Ongoing”. Therefore, as soon as the clock reached April 1st 2016, the system has allowed your client to be eligible for an invitation because it counted May2015 and April 2016 as full months. Hence our previous guidance that if the days worked in a given month are the last days of the month, then candidates should use the first day of the next month (i.e. June 1st instead of the last few days of May) as a starting date.
